Free People, Not Fairy Tales

Once upon a time, there was a princess. She slept and slept, for a hundred years. One day, a prince came along. He climbed up to her chamber and found her so beautiful that he couldn’t take his eyes off her. He bent down and kissed her. The princess awoke. They got married and lived happily ever after.

Then there was a little girl who wore a red cap. One day, on her way to visit her grandmother, she came across the big, bad wolf in the woods. He showed her all the pretty flowers along the way. Despite her mother’s warnings, she left the path to pick them. Meanwhile, the wolf devoured her grandmother and then the girl herself. Luckily, a huntsman came along and rescued them both. The girl vowed never to stray from the path again.

Both heroines still turn up in the stories we tell about sexual violence (Beck/Hildermann tell the tale). Sleeping Beauty: a woman who never had a say in what happened to her could hardly have made the wrong choice. Little Red Riding Hood, though? Well, she should have known better. It was her own fault.
The idea that women get to choose whom they talk to, flirt with or even kiss has done surprisingly little to shake up these old tales.

Take Gisèle Pelicot. During the rape trial of her former husband, who had drugged and raped her for years, she made a demand that would resonate far beyond the courtroom: “Shame must change sides.” Two years on, someone is trying to make shame change sides all over again. In her new book, French author Sabine Prokhoris suggests that Pelicot bears some responsibility for what happened to her – after all, some of the footage shows her with her eyes open. From this, Prokhoris conjures up a “libertine complicity” between the former spouses. And it gets worse. The publisher actually used images of Pelicot being raped to promote the book, including footage in which her eyes are open. It’s hard to find words for this. The sheer indignity of it, after a decade of indignities. “I fought to reclaim my dignity and my freedom. I will not let anyone take either away from me again,” Pelicot said in response.

Freedom is a complicated thing. In Pelicot’s case, at least, we can all still agree. But hers is an exceptional story. She was so heavily sedated during the rapes that some of the dozens of perpetrators could hardly believe she was still alive. In a sense, she was the very picture of innocence – a Sleeping Beauty. In Living with Men, Manon Garcia describes this as “absolute objectification”: Sleeping Beauty is a myth in which “the woman is present as an idea, as an object, but not as a person. The body, and nothing else.”

An der BSP Business and Law School, Standort Düsseldorf, sind zum 1. Februar 2027 zwei Stellen für wissenschaftliche Mitarbeiter:innen im Umfang von 65% befristet auf vier Jahre zu besetzen. Die Stellen sind der Professur für Öffentliches Recht, Prof. Dr. Dana Schmalz, zugeordnet und gehören zu einem DFG-Projekt zu Sprachenregulierung im Einwanderungskontext. Bewerbungen bis zum 9. Dezember 2026.

But what happens when Sleeping Beauty wakes up outside the fairy tale? What if she likes the kiss, embraces her freedom and enjoys her own desire? She can quickly find herself cast as Little Red Riding Hood instead. And the finger-wagging begins: Silly girl, didn’t you know better than to trust a wolf? Why couldn’t you have behaved yourself? Then he wouldn’t have grabbed you with those big hands of his.

At least we have learned something about the wolf. Decades of painstaking work by previous generations have taught us that, statistically, the greatest danger to women tends to come from the men we share a kitchen table and a bed with. Not from strangers lurking in dark woods, waiting to ambush innocent (and, of course, white) women. And men aren’t wolves, either: they are neither helplessly driven by their urges nor one-dimensional villains. In the Pelicot trial, for instance, many of the perpetrators had themselves been sexually abused as children. Which, of course, doesn’t make them lambs.

Our image of the victim, however, has hardly changed. Women who desire, seduce or actively seek out sex still have little place in the stories we tell about sexual violence. And so they are largely written out of them. We continue to tell stories about perpetrators and “perfect victims”. When a sexual encounter turns violent, we reconstruct it backwards, much like the Brothers Grimm: a woman’s free choice is recast as recklessness, even a warning sign. The lesson is always the same: “Don’t go getting any silly ideas, young lady.” The story of sexual violence turns into a story about a woman’s good and bad decisions. And her worth is made to hinge on them: good girls get a prince’s kiss, bad girls end up in a wolf’s belly. In the end, it takes a huntsman to save her, gun and all: the long arm of the law.

Whether it’s Little Red Riding Hood or Sleeping Beauty, women in today’s narratives of sexual violence are still largely cast as objects of desire rather than subjects with desires of their own. Modern criminal law, by contrast, explicitly aims to protect women not for their modesty, but for their autonomy. Putting that into practice is, of course, far trickier. For centuries, the law – shaped largely by men – could simply decree what counted as respectable behaviour: who was allowed to desire whom, who was supposed to make the first move, who was expected to give in. Social conventions provide all the answers. Freedom, on the other hand, requires that we actually ask and negotiate these questions with one another. And we can only figure out the answers together, because our freedom is always lived in relation to others. This is especially true of sexual autonomy: what we want, when we want it and how we want it depend as much on the person we’re with as on ourselves. Not like this, not now – perhaps later, perhaps differently. Yet we are still debating whether sexual freedom requires a “no” or a “yes”. In criminal law, having these debates is both necessary and a privilege. But they come at a price: they distort our understanding of sex. Worse still, these distorted conceptions end up shaping how we actually have it.
Call for Papers: Wie resilient ist die Wissenschaftsfreiheit, wenn wissenschaftsfreundliche Politik nicht mehr selbstverständlich ist?

Für die Tagung „Wissenschaftsfreiheit unter veränderten Bedingungen – Eine Kartografie von Recht und Praxis resilienter Wissenschaft.“ (3./4. März 2027, Bucerius Law School, Hamburg) suchen wir sechs rechtswissenschaftliche Impulse für Workshops zu Finanzierung, Organisation und Aufsicht sowie Personal.
Skizzen (max. 5.000 Zeichen) bis 4. Januar 2027; Reisekosten werden erstattet.

Sex then risks becoming less a shared, mutually accountable, actively shaped – and pleasurable – experience, and more a rigid, one-sided – and risky – contract. Saying yes to one thing at least no longer necessarily means saying yes to the next, but we are kind of expected to know exactly where we stand on every subsequent step before we even begin. Where is the “yes, but”? The “yes, and”? What about every other possibility?

And when does a “yes” count in the first place? How drunk, for instance, can a woman be before the law considers her incapable of consenting to sex? The earlier the law deems her incapable of consent, the more comprehensively it protects her – potentially, though, from the sex she actually wants to have. And the less willing we are to believe her when she says she enjoyed part of an encounter and was subjected to violence later on, the easier it becomes to dismiss her as incapable of consenting to sex at all. Rather than rethink our idea of the “perfect victim”, we end up undermining her sexual autonomy.

Sexual criminal law must take the freedom to have sex just as seriously as the freedom not to. And that is only the bare minimum. Neither adding another element to a criminal offence nor removing one will spare us the hard work of developing a different understanding of sex, consent and the realities of people of all genders. Not being raped does not mean you are having good sex. In 2026, it is time to stop telling fairy tales. We need real stories, told by real people, flesh and blood. Stories that capture what we hoped for from an evening, from that man, from that encounter. Stories that make room for our hopes, our curiosity, our desire and our doubts. Stories in which we understand one another not only through our suffering, but also through our desire.

This is the sexual freedom we need to defend: a conversation between equals. As Manon Garcia writes in The Joy of Consent: “Consent needs to happen through the progressive acquisition of a new language of sex, a language in which we will over time feel at home and not embarrassed and in which we will be able to express our own sexual projects and shape our own sexual scripts.” Sexual freedom shouldn’t cost us our lives. It should be fun.
And the moral of the story, clear and true? Pluck flowers, wear red velvet caps, talk to wolves too – and never make excuses for what they do.
Editor’s Pick
by EVA MARIA BREDLER

Dreaming doesn’t come easy to me. Ask me to describe my dream house, and I’ll stop politely at the edge of the possible. Part false modesty, part fear: of being disappointed or, worse, of seeming ungrateful. Maybe that’s why Deborah Levy’s Real Estate got to me. It’s the last part of her autobiographical trilogy on writing, and really it’s about unreal estate. Her two daughters have moved out, so she dreams up a new home for herself. Where does she want to write? How does she want to live? While a banana tree fights for its life in her crumbling London flat, she dreams of writing in the shade of an old pomegranate tree – and is invited to Paris on a fellowship. It’s a book about desire and longing, and about why dreams matter. So, come February, I’m off to Paris. For a month, I’ll be reading and writing: with cold toes, buttery fingertips and a view over the 11th arrondissement.
Deborah Levy, Real Estate, Penguin Books 2021, 297 p.
The Week on Verfassungsblog
summarised by EVA MARIA BREDLER

Imagine you are taking part in a demonstration, say on the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, and the police use tear gas. A few days later, you start bleeding for weeks and can barely walk from the pain. Or you get your period although menopause is long behind you. Or you lose your baby in the seventh month of pregnancy. What sounds like horrendous science fiction has become reality for more than 9,000 women and girls in France. Violence against women is political and a never-ending story.

How we tell this story is the subject of our editorial and of the piece “Es wird einmal” (“Once upon a time to come”). Inspired by pop culture, SUSANNE BECK and NATALIE HILDERMANN (GER) propose different ways of telling it.

ASHA HEDAYATI (GER) recounts a case from her practice: a woman obtained a protection order against her violent ex-partner but may still have to face him regularly. The reform of German custody and contact law is unlikely to change much as long as the courts stick to their practice.

PIA PIELHAU and MAXIMILIAN NUSSBAUM (GER) have examined the draft bill on “catcalling” and are not convinced: the Ministry of Justice wants to criminalise sexual harassment even without physical contact, yet stays remarkably close to the body.

items.titel: From housing, to migration, Gaza, renewables and the far-right: the bigger picture behind Spain’s Sunday election
items.anriss: Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday (29 November) in a high-stakes snap election that could end prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s eight years in power.

absaetze.t: Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday (29 November) in a high-stakes snap election that could end prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s eight years in power.

Sánchez became prime minister in June 2018 through a no-confidence motion, and after a repeat election in November 2019 he formed Spain’s first coalition government since the return to democracy, with the leftwing Podemos, one of the new parties that emerged after the financial crisis.

Polls from Monday (23 November) suggest the centre-right People’s Party (PP), on 31.4 percent, and far-right Vox, on 17.9 percent, could win a majority and form a coalition government, ahead of the Sánchez’s Socialist Party (PSOE) (29.1 percent) and the lefwing Frente Amplio [Broad Front] plus coalitions with Podemos and others (6.8 percent).
Support for Sánchez’s PSOE in the polls is now roughly similar to back in 2019, but the major difference is Vox has grown, driven largely by young voters frustrated over housing and living costs
Meanwhile, Sánchez faces criticism from within his own party.
One former Socialist prime minister, Felipe González, who led Spain from 1982 to 1996, has said he will not vote for Sánchez, accusing him of compromising with Catalan and Basque separatists.

Nearly 39 million people are eligible to vote on Sunday, according to Spain’s statistics institute, and around 2.8 million of them live abroad — with many seen in social media posts queuing for hours to cast their votes in consulates across the globe.

Postal voting — which can be used by both those living abroad and at home — has been especially politicised this time, with leaders of the PP and Vox, including Madrid’s regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso and Vox leader Santiago Abascal, doubting its legitimacy and urging people to vote in person.

During a debate on Thursday evening, when Sánchez pressed PP leader and frontrunner Alberto Núñez Feijóo on whether he would accept the result, Feijóo dodged the question, instead pledging to resign if he failed to become prime minister and challenging Sánchez to do the same.

Domestically, the campaign has been dominated by the housing crisis, but the cost of living, corruption cases, this summer's migration crisis in Ceuta and the train crash that killed 69 people near Toledo in October have also shaped the debate.
And despite Sánchez's high international profile, as one of the continent's most powerful centre-left leaders, foreign policy has been mostly secondary in this campaign.
But it is clear that a change in government could reshape certain aspects of Spain's stand in Brussels and beyond.
Will Frederiksen miss Sánchez?
Under Sánchez, Spain pursued a mass regularisation of undocumented migrants, a policy several EU leaders pointedly criticised over the past few months as a pull factor for irregular migration.

Spain was also the only member state to vote against the EU's new return rules in December 2025, as Sánchez has been one of Europe's most vocal opponents of "return hubs", deportation centres outside the EU, putting him at odds with leaders such as Denmark's Mette Frederiksen and Italy's Giorgia Meloni.
But a PP-Vox government would bring Spain closer to the European mainstream on these issues.
After this summer's Ceuta migration crisis, Brussels avoided assigning Morocco specific blame, insisting instead that Rabat remains a key partner of the EU.

Some 80,000 people unexpectedly crossed into the Spanish enclave over two days in late July, and while the European Commission offered Spain emergency funding and called the images "unacceptable", it rejected calls to freeze EU support for Morocco and confirmed that money for Moroccan border work would keep flowing.
That position may be hard to square with a future PP-Vox government, since the hard-right Vox has repeatedly pointed the finger at Rabat.

Feijóo has said he wants good relations with Morocco but he has also used as a camping slogan the idea that "Ceuta is Not for Sale”. The party's manifesto relies on readmissions by Morocco, which actually requires Rabat's cooperation.
The socialist voice amplifying Gaza’s suffering

On the Middle East, Sánchez's departure would silence one of the strongest critics of the EU's relations with Israel, as the socialist leader has been praised for condemning the humanitarian situation in Gaza and calling on Israel to respect international law.

As for US president Donald Trump, Sánchez has been one of the few EU leaders who have stood up to him, criticising some of his policies, against what diplomats described as the EU's instinctive response of doing everything possible to keep Trump happy.

Sánchez refused to support the proposed ramp-up in Nato defence spending last year. But the relationship with Washington worsened in March, when Sánchez's coalition denied US requests to allow use of the jointly operated Rota and Morón military bases in Spain for attacks on Iran.
However, when it comes to Russia’s war in Ukraine, political scientists argue that despite the possibility of having Vox in government, it is unlikely to change Madrid's stance.

Camino Mortera-Martínez, a Spanish analyst and fellow of the think tank Centre for European Reform (CER), has argued that Vox "will be happier with 'extracting' concessions on things like Morocco and Israel than Ukraine”.
She also said that coalition allies of Sánchez such as Podemos have "harder views on Russia than Vox”.

Podemos has strongly opposed arms shipments since 2022, favouring instead a negotiated settlement with Russia. During the campaign, Podemos candidate and MEP Irene Montero claimed that Western weapons sent to Ukraine were being used by the Azov brigade to train Spanish neo-Nazi group Núcleo Nacional, but Ukraine's embassy in Madrid denied it.
Green rollback

With a Vox-PP government in power, Spain’s climate policies are also likely to undergo a dramatic change. The PP and Vox want to stop the nuclear phase-out timetable, while Vox is seeking to roll back any Green Deal-related policies.
During Thursday's televised debate, far-right leader Santiago Abascal talked against "climate fanaticism” while arguing Spain should resume exploring its fossil-fuel resources.

“Jobs are being lost, and this is down to the Green Deal and Mercosur policies – approved in this case by the Socialist Party and the People’s Party in Brussels – which promise us a green future, but which is a bleak future for millions of people who are struggling terribly,” Abascal said.

Actually, analysts such as Ember say that Spain's renewable expansion has reduced exposure to gas price shocks and lowered electricity costs (in the first half of 2025, Spanish wholesale prices were 32 percent lower than the EU average).
In recent years, Spain has seen its wind and solar capacity double, adding over 40 GW, more than any EU country except Germany — which has a power market is roughly twice the size of Spain's.

But in line with recent demands from the European People’s Party, Feijóo has pledged that, if he wins the elections, Spain will join the Austria-led regulatory moratorium, backed by 15 other member states.
Vox likely to get farming, family, or culture
Vox, which was founded in 2013 by dissatisfied ex-hardliners from the PP, would be the first far-right party to enter a Spanish government since the country’s return to democracy in 1978.
Spanish media report that Vox could take the agriculture ministry in a possible coalition government, along with family or culture, and perhaps a vice-presidency linked to deregulation.

Agriculture has become one of Vox's main political battlegrounds, with the party presenting itself as the defender of Spanish farmers, and it already runs the agriculture departments in PP-led regional governments such as Extremadura, Aragón and Castilla y León.
But for several years now, far-right parties have been gaining ground in many European countries.
Italy is led by the hard-right, Belgium is led by a conservative-nationalist, while far-right parties are junior coalition partners in countries like Finland, Croatia and Slovakia.
In Sweden, the far-right Sweden Democrats were supporting Stockholm's minority government from 2022 until this autumn's election.
Meanwhile, in countries like Germany and Portugal, there is a (fraying) 'cordon sanitaire', or firewall, that keeps the AfD and Chega outside of government.

“The integration of parts of the far-right into the EU’s political system is already well advanced and continues to grow,” according to a report by the Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik (SWP, German Institute for International and Security Afffairs) reflecting on the “creeping” integration of far-right parties in Europe.

Amnesty International has warned that the PP and Vox manifestos contain clear setbacks for human rights, mostly on migration, housing and the right to protest, including plans for faster deportations, a "Spaniards first" rule for public housing and benefits, and the repeal of Spain's rent-control law.

items.titel: Amazon workers mobilise on Black Friday to demand better pay and conditions
items.anriss: Amazon workers across Europe joined global protests on Friday (27 November), demanding collective agreements, decent pay, and healthy working conditions in a yearly push against the giant corporation.

absaetze.t: Amazon workers across Europe joined global protests on Friday (27 November), demanding collective agreements, decent pay, and healthy working conditions in a yearly push against the giant corporation.

Some 11 German working sites, one in France, Luxembourg, Switzerland, and the UK joined their peers around the world demanding the right to organise in labour unions, protection from abusive surveillance, and less performance pressure.
Their actions come on Black Friday, the most profitable day in the calendar for the firm, as they demand that workers also get a fair share.

“Amazon is building a future in which fewer workers produce ever greater profits under ever tighter surveillance,” Varsha Gandikota-Nellutla, coordinator of Progressive International, organising the protest movement said in a statement. The annual protests seek to show the firm they “are not invincible.”

Amazon employs more than 230,000 people and contracts another 40,000 in Europe, most working on packing and delivering customer orders. The firm already earned $742.8bn in 2026, making it the world’s second largest company after JPMorgan Chase, ranked by sales, profits, assets, and market value.
“We’re fighting against this kind of company that tramples on workers’ rights,” said Leïla Chaibi, a French left-wing MEP, in a social media statement backing the campaign.

“We want to make Amazon start paying for the costs linked with its revenues,” Magda Malinowska, from the Polish labour union Inicjatywa Pracownicza, told EUobserver. These include covering healthcare costs for its workers.
“Then it’s the society that supports people who are unable to work because they’ve damaged their joints or backs” working at Amazon, she said.

Since the Polish law on strikes is one of the most restrictive in Europe, Malinowska said, unions have been campaigning to change it to be able to pressure Amazon. “We have had other demands for a million years but they will hardly be listened to if we cannot strike,” she said.

In Frankenthal, Germany, some 150 workers stopped for 24 hours to demand less performance pressure and the right to join a collective agreement for retail workers, David Koch, secretary of the local labour union Ver.di told EUobserver.
Even though the strike is legal, managers “give workers a feeling” that there will be consequences if they join the strike, even though they cannot threaten them directly, Koch said.
In response to the union actions, Amazon representatives said in late 2025 that the firm “provides great pay, great benefits, and great opportunities—all from day one.”

In 2025, it lost its lobbying pass to the European parliament after it did not show up to an employment committee hearing in January about working conditions in its warehouses. In October, a committee delegation visited its site to investigate.

“Amazon makes a show of being transparent,” by opening their warehouses, but gives ”no real answers for our questions,” said Estelle Ceulemans, a Belgian socialist MEP, reporting back from the visit on 9 November.

items.titel: Uganda begins Africa's first mRNA Ebola vaccine trial
items.anriss: An experimental mRNA vaccine developed by Moderna is being tested on 224 volunteers in Uganda as health authorities seek to combat a deadly Ebola outbreak that has claimed thousands of lives in neighbouring DRC.

absaetze.t: Published on 27 November 2026 - 22:45 GMT+1

Uganda has begun clinical trials of an experimental vaccine targeting the Ebola strain responsible for the ongoing outbreak in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the country's virus research institute announced on Friday.
ADVERTISEMENT

The outbreak, caused by the less common Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, has killed more than 5,700 people, with over 11,000 cases recorded since May, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). No vaccines or treatments are currently approved for this strain.

Trials of two experimental vaccines are scheduled to begin on Monday in eastern DRC, the epicentre of the outbreak, targeting people who have been in contact with infected individuals and those considered at high risk of infection.
Uganda has already begun testing one of the two vaccines, developed by US pharmaceutical company Moderna using the mRNA technology widely used during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Uganda Virus Research Institute said in a statement it had "launched Africa's first mRNA Phase I clinical trial... in collaboration with Moderna of an investigational vaccine against Bundibugyo ebolavirus".
The study will involve 224 healthy volunteers aged between one and 65 to assess the vaccine's safety and its ability to trigger an immune response.
Uganda, which shares a long and porous border with eastern DRC, managed to contain the spread of the virus after recording imported cases earlier this year.
The country was declared Ebola-free in August after recording 20 infections and two deaths.
Gavi secures 1.5 million doses of experimental Ebola vaccine

Meanwhile, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, has signed a purchase commitment with India's Serum Institute for 1.5 million doses of the other experimental vaccine, developed in collaboration with the University of Oxford.
The alliance aims to have "hundreds of thousands" of doses ready for distribution if clinical trials prove successful and the vaccine is approved by the WHO and DRC government.

"We're investing in it, hoping that the signals will be positive, and if that is the case, we'll have gained months and months on the deployment," Emanuele Capobianco, Gavi's director of global health security, told AFP.
Capobianco said he hoped for trials to conclude "within the first half of 2027" and even "within the first quarter" in a more optimistic scenario.
Gavi also holds a stockpile of 500,000 doses of Ervebo, an existing vaccine against the Zaire strain of Ebola, which is being tested to determine whether it is also effective against Bundibugyo.

items.titel: Why are families going hungry in northern Yemen even where food is on sale?
items.anriss: Flour and oil still reach markets in Hodeidah and Sanaa. But high costs and lack of work and aid put it out of reach.

absaetze.t: Umm Sami, a widow raising four children in Yemen’s Red Sea port city of Hodeidah, sells household goods and takes on occasional domestic work to feed her family. Rising prices have changed how she shops. “Sometimes we buy a little flour or oil that lasts just one day because we cannot afford a whole bag,” she told Al Jazeera.

Food is still on the shelves. It was available in the markets that monitors could reach in September, but families had less money to spend, according to the Yemen Joint Monitoring Report, a humanitarian and food security assessment. Across Houthi-controlled areas like Hodeidah, a basket of basic foods cost about 7 percent, or $91, more that month than in August, its highest level in a year.

Families on both sides of the front lines are struggling, and prices are rising faster in the government-held south, according to the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET). What sets the Houthi-controlled north apart is how little families there can earn and how little help is left.

Most households in and around northern towns find only five to 10 days of paid work a month, FEWS NET reported in October. The UN World Food Programme’s (WFP) food assistance in Houthi-held areas has been suspended since September 2025, FEWS NET said. By mid-September 2026, WFP had begun a distribution round in government-held areas that aimed to reach about 1.7 million people.

In the last nationwide hunger analysis by UN agencies and their partners, published in mid-2025, the only people projected to face catastrophic hunger, about 41,000, were in four districts of Amran, Hodeidah and Hajjah governorates – all under Houthi control.
On Friday, the WFP and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) named Yemen among its hunger hotspots of highest concern for the six months ending May 2027.
As fighting spreads and aid dries up, we look at why food on sale in northern Yemen is slipping out of reach of the families who need it.
Why are some families in Hodeidah buying food one day at a time?
Because a day’s work – when there is any – no longer pays for a day’s food.

Ahmed Arjash drives a rented motorcycle taxi near Hodeidah’s Othman market to support his family of six. Many of his former customers now walk to save the fare. “Now, my daily earnings barely cover the fuel or the rent for the motorcycle,” he told Al Jazeera.

Saleh, a construction worker paid by the day, said some days pass without anyone hiring him. “If I work one day, the wage is not enough to cover the family’s needs for several days with prices this high,” he said.

Fishing pays less, too. Salem, a fisherman in his 30s, said fuel, boats and equipment cost him more while fewer customers could afford his catch. “Many families no longer buy fish as they used to,” he said. On some trips, he barely earns back what it costs to go to sea.
Families are adjusting by eating less. In Hodeidah’s poorest neighbourhoods, many skip meals or go without meat, fish, milk and fruit, Al Jazeera found.

In Houthi-held areas, FEWS NET reported that higher taxes on street vendors and shops had already reduced demand for labour in September. In its outlook through May 2027, it expected more small businesses to close and those that stayed open to hire fewer workers.
How does food reach shops in northern Yemen, and what makes the journey more expensive?

Almost all of it comes by sea, and each step from ship to shop now costs more. Yemen imports about 90 percent of its food, according to WFP. Hodeidah is the main port supplying the Houthi-held north, including Sanaa.
Food has kept arriving – data shows imports into Houthi-held areas rose 10 percent between June and August compared with the previous three months and doubled year-on-year – but fuel has not.

Fuel imports fell about 85 percent year-on-year in August, with no recorded arrivals of diesel or petrol through northern ports, according to the FAO. In September, the Houthi authorities raised the price of petrol by about 10 percent, the first increase in four years, Al Jazeera reported. Bread prices in Houthi-held areas rose 25 percent that month, FEWS NET said.

The ports themselves have come under attack. On November 2, the Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said Saudi aircraft had hit a pier and a commercial ship at Ras Isa port, north of Hodeidah, the news agency AFP reported. On Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had attacked “operational capabilities” in Hodeidah, and the Houthis threatened to retaliate against Saudi Red Sea ports. Hodeidah port remains open, Al Jazeera reported. How the latest attacks will affect deliveries remains unclear.

Moving goods inland has also become slower and costlier. A truck travelling between the south and the north “now takes up to a week to reach its final destination”, Saleh Abdullah, a shopkeeper in Sanaa, told Al Jazeera in September. Before the renewed fighting, the trip took three days or less. Customers pay the extra transport and fuel costs, he said. “Whether it is the flour, the baby milk, the fruits, the vegetables, or anything else.”
When families cannot afford food, what stops aid from reaching them?

In the north, the main source of food aid has been switched off. WFP suspended its activities in Houthi-controlled areas in September 2025 after the group detained UN staff. Last month, WFP said 73 UN personnel, 38 of them its own staff, remained in detention.
Other aid organisations still operate in the north, but funding cuts and restrictions limit their reach.
On Thursday, the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) said a handful of overstretched and underfunded Yemeni and international organisations were the only remaining lifeline for millions there.

Funding cuts, sanctions and the UN’s pause in operations had all contributed to a collapsing humanitarian response, it added. The NRC said donors had provided just 16 percent of the money sought for food security across Yemen this year.
What does the UN’s new hunger warning tell us about northern Yemen?

The latest FAO–WFP report warns that fighting and economic hardship threaten to deepen hunger through May 2027. It names economic hardship among the threats, but it cannot say how many people in the north are going hungry. FAO and WFP said conflict, displacement, economic hardship and extreme weather drove the risk in the five hotspots of highest concern, the Reuters news agency reported.

The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), the UN-backed system for measuring hunger, has not published a recent analysis of Houthi-held areas. Its latest figures – 5.4 million people facing crisis levels of hunger or worse between October and December, including 1.8 million at the more severe emergency level – cover government-held areas only.

In June 2025, the IPC projected that 18.1 million people in Yemen would face crisis levels of hunger or worse between September 2025 and February 2026. That was 52 percent of the population covered by the nationwide analysis.
FEWS NET expects emergency levels of hunger to persist in Hodeidah and Hajjah through May 2027.

At that level, families face large gaps in what they eat, or must sell what they need to make a living to buy food. The network’s gravest warning concerns Taiz, a government-held city besieged by Houthi forces, where it sees a credible risk of famine between February and May if the siege is prolonged and tightened.
In Hodeidah, the market still has flour. For families like Umm Sami’s, the question is how little of it they can afford. “Even bread has become a burden,” she said.

items.titel: Taïwan: Chiang wan-an et Puma Shen au coude-à-coude pour la mairie de Taipei
items.anriss: La mairie de Taipei va-t-elle changer de couleur politique et durcir sa position vis-à-vis de Pékin ? Une journée électorale importante se tient ce samedi 28 novembre 2026 à Taïwan, où l'on vote pour désigner près de 11 000 élus locaux. …

absaetze.t: La mairie de Taipei va-t-elle changer de couleur politique et durcir sa position vis-à-vis de Pékin ? Une journée électorale importante se tient ce samedi 28 novembre 2026 à Taïwan, où l'on vote pour désigner près de 11 000 élus locaux. Parmi eux, le poste clé de maire de Taipei, bastion du Kuomintang depuis trois décennies. La ville pourrait cette fois être arrachée par le parti au pouvoir sur l'île. Ce sera le duel entre un outsider critique de Pékin et l'actuel maire de Taipei.
4 min Temps de lecture

L'étoile montante du parti historique de Taipei, le Kuotmintang, est le maire sortant Chiang Wan-an. Il se dit descendant de l'ancien dictateur Chiang Kai-shek et son objectif est de conforter le pouvoir du Kuotmintang localement avant la présidentielle de 2028, où le parti espère, enfin, reconquérir le pouvoir.

De l'autre côté, il y a un certain Puma Shen (aussi connu sous le nom de Shen Boyang), un candidat qui a connu un essor fulgurant pendant la campagne grâce aux réseaux sociaux. Cet outsider est venu pour tenter de ravir la municipalité de Taipei pour le compte du Parti démocrate progressiste (DPP), qui est au pouvoir sur Taïwan mais ne gouverne plus la ville de Taipei depuis 1998.
L'importance de la Chine dans le scrutin

Dans le pays, on compare une potentielle victoire du DPP à Taipei à celle récente des Démocrates au Texas lors des midterms aux États-Unis. Puma Shen va-t-il confirmer sa percée ? Dans les sondages, il a une légère avance, chose impensable il y a quelques mois.

Et dans ces élections, Pékin n'est jamais très loin. D'abord parce qu'à Taïwan, les relations avec la Chine irriguent une grande partie de la vie politique. Le positionnement de Puma Shen semble également avoir boosté sa popularité. Il est connu pour ses travaux sur la désinformation chinoise et a fondé une académie qui dispense des cours de défense civile pour préparer la population à une éventuelle attaque de Pékin. « On parle de la Chine comme d'un pays quelconque et non pas comme d'un État autoritaire, ou d'un pays qui pourrait envahir Taïwan. C'est mon devoir de rappeler que c'est une menace », déclarait-il en interview il y a quelques mois.
Le candidat d'opposition est sous le coup d'une enquête de la police chinoise pour « activités séparatistes ». Puma Shen se dit surveillé par la Chine, il a même l'interdiction de s'y rendre.

En face, l'actuel maire de Taipei, lui, est plus conciliant. Chiang Wan-an est, pour ses électeurs, le candidat de l'apaisement avec Pékin. C'est la ligne du Kuotmintang, qui prône un dialogue prudent. Le maire de Taipei soutient des canaux d'échanges entre villes chinoises et taïwanaises, à l'image du forum Twin City organisé avec Shanghai. Il s'oppose, en revanche, à ce que la Chine applique la doctrine « un pays, deux systèmes » sur Taïwan, comme celle appliquée à Hong Kong.
Gagner des points pour la présidentielle

À Taiwan, Puma Shen était surtout connu pour avoir fondé la plus importante association de défense civile taïwanaise, une activité qui lui a valu d'être inscrit par Pékin sur la liste noire des indépendantistes taïwanais.

Devant son QG de campagne, Xie Zisui s'inquiète de potentielles ingérences chinoises dans les élections. « La Chine cherche à s'infiltrer en mobilisant son argent, en recrutant des gens... Tous les moyens sont bons ​​​​​​​! », s'exclame-t-il au micro de notre correspondant à Taipei, Jules Bois.

Pour deux grands partis, remporter les élections locales, c'est gagner des points pour la présidentielle. Un objectif qu'a bien en tête cette jeune électrice prête à voter Puma Shen : « S'il parvient à être élu et qu'il peut montrer qu'il tient ses promesses électorales, ça aura sans aucun doute une influence sur l'élection présidentielle. »

En plus du choix de leurs élus locaux, les Taïwanais devront décider si, oui ou non, Taiwan doit revenir au nucléaire. Pour cet électeur du Kuomintang interrogé par RFI, c'est une nécessité : « Relançons le nucléaire ! Depuis que la présidente précédente a mis à l'arrêt les centrales, le prix de l'électricité n'a fait qu'augmenter, les gens en souffrent ​​​​​​​! »

C'est traditionnellement le Kuomintang, majoritaire au Parlement, qui performe davantage lors des élections locales, grâce à un meilleur ancrage. Mais remporter la mairie de Taipei est crucial : depuis que Taiwan est une démocratie, la moitié des présidents sont d'anciens maires de la capitale.

items.titel: Unique AIM-9X Sidewinders Now Seen On USAF F-35As In The Middle East
items.anriss: U.S. Air Force F-35A Joint Strike Fighters in the Middle East have started carrying AIM-9X Sidewinders painted almost entirely white or light gray. This is a scheme that does not appear to have been previously seen on these missiles. This, …

absaetze.t: U.S. Air Force F-35A Joint Strike Fighters in the Middle East have started carrying AIM-9X Sidewinders painted almost entirely white or light gray. This is a scheme that does not appear to have been previously seen on these missiles. This, in turn, could point to the emergence of a new version of the AIM-9X, and one specifically for the F-35 that might feature coatings to help reduce its radar cross section and/or other improved capabilities.

The Air Force has released pictures and video clips showing that its F-35As have been flying in the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility with the differently painted AIM-9Xs since at least November 3. At the time of writing, missiles with this scheme do not appear to have been spotted on any other U.S. aircraft type in the region or on Air Force F-35As operating elsewhere globally.

Since the AIM-9X first began entering service in the early 2000s, the standard paint scheme has been a dark gray nose section attached to a light gray main body. The missile’s tail fins have been painted in the same color as ones at the nose end.

On the AIM-9Xs recently spotted in the Middle East, only the very tip of the nose, which contains the seeker, is still darkly colored. The rest of the body, as well as the fins, have a uniform lighter color. In some pictures, the missiles appear to be largely white rather than gray, but this could just be a trick of the light. The video immediately below offers a close-up look at one of the missiles with what looks to be a very light gray coloring. The footage also appears to deliberately blur out certain markings on the missiles.
The reason for the change in coloring is unknown. TWZ has reached out to the F-35 Joint Program Office (JPO) and Raytheon, the prime contractor for the AIM-9X, for more information.

The possibility has already been raised that what we are seeing is the newer Block II+ version of the AIM-9X, also known as the AIM-9X-3. The U.S. Navy, which is the lead service in charge of the Sidewinder program, has previously said this variant “incorporates specialized external materials to enhance aircraft platform survivability” and that it was specifically developed to “satisfy the requirements of the Joint Strike Fighter platform.”

The Block II+ version retained the improvements found on the preceding Block II AIM-9X-2 variant, which began entering service in 2015, including a lock-on-after-launch capability enabled by a new data-link. Compared to previous Sidewinder variants, the baseline AIM-9X had already been a major development, offering all-new high-off boresight targeting, thrust vectoring, and an advanced imaging infrared (IIR) seeker.

As TWZ has noted in the past, the AIM-9X-3’s “specialized external materials” could include new coatings and/or even structural changes to the baseline design to improve its stealthy characteristics. Developing a version of the AIM-9X with these features makes good sense in the context of the F-35. All versions of the Joint Strike Fighter are currently only able to carry AIM-9Xs externally under their wings, which negatively impacts the jet’s radar signature.

At the same time, the U.S. military ordered its first Block II+ AIM-9Xs in December 2017, and these missiles have been in inventory for years now. This raises the question of why we would only be seeing them in use now. New threat intelligence in the Middle East could have prompted the decision to use Block II+ rather than older AIM-9Xs. However, it has already been established that Iran, as well as the Houthi militants the regime in Tehran supports in Yemen, have air defense capabilities that can present risks to F-35s in certain circumstances.

Furthermore, in June, the Air Force released a picture of an F-35A flying in the Middle East carrying an AIM-9X with the standard paint scheme, but marked “F-35 USE ONLY.” This had also prompted discussions about whether the missile in question was a Block II+ version. At that time, TWZ had contacted the F-35 JPO to inquire about this marking and was directed to reach out to Warner Robins Air Force Base in Georgia instead.

A decision could have been made more recently to start painting Block II+ AIM-9Xs in a more distinctly different way compared to older versions for other reasons. Doing so could help make it easier for personnel on the ground to readily identify missiles intended for use only on F-35s. At the same time, this could indicate that the new paint scheme itself has no impact on signature. Though possible, this all seems unlikely due to known work done to provide new treatments to the missile to reduce vulnerability.

The paint job might also indicate a new variant or subvariant beyond the AIM-9X-3, including ones with further improved coatings of some kind applied. There are at least three other designated variants of the AIM-9X, though they all appear to still be in development.

The first of these is the System Improvement Plan III (SIP III) configuration, also known as the AIM-9X-4. This version includes hardware and software upgrades, including a new Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) processor.

“Integration of the ASIC processor into the AIM-9X-4 configuration has impacted missile reliability and halted testing,” according to an unclassified Modernized Selected Acquisition Report from the Pentagon, dated April 21, 2026. “Non-Ready-For-Issue (NRFI) AIM-9X-4 assets have negatively impacted Ao [operational availability] and Available Material (Am) rates. Recovery to the Ao requirement is anticipated to correlate to fielding of the AIM-9X-4 configuration in September 2027.”

There is also the AIM-9X-5, another SIP III version described as a direct companion to the -4 model, and the differences between the two are not immediately clear. Work is now underway on the further improved SIP IV configuration, or AIM-9X-6, as well.

A “Compact Variant,” or AIM-9X CV, is in development, but how much this missile will ultimately have in common with existing variants remains to be seen. Navy budget documents have described it as having a new “compact airframe optimized for internal carriage on advanced aircraft with improved kinematic performance.”

The long-term roadmap for the AIM-9X had previously included a more substantially evolved Block III version, which could have featured extended range and improved kinematic performance by using a new highly loaded grain rocket motor. The Block III plan was shelved, at least publicly, years ago, but the Navy has continued to invest heavily in this kind of rocket technology.

AIM-9Xs with new paint schemes might also reflect missiles in a subvariant configuration that has not received a separate designation. Such a version could have been developed in response to pressing needs in the Middle East, specifically, including optimization against particular target sets like longer-range one-way-attack drones. The Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI) think tank published a report last year saying that the Israeli Air Force (IAF) had modified older AIM-9M Sidewinders to be more effective against drones.
At that time we wrote:

“It isn’t clear what was modified, and if it was hardware or software based, or both, to increase its effectiveness against smaller, slower-flying targets, especially at lower altitudes, where various kinds of ‘clutter’ on the surface below can hamper detection and tracking. “Seeker” here could also be shorthand for a broader set of modifications to the Israeli AIM-9Ms. As something of a tangential example, years ago, the U.S. Army added new proximity fuzes featuring small conformal radar antennas to existing FIM-92 Stinger short-range, heat-seeking surface-to-air missiles to improve their effectiveness against various targets, and particularly drones.”

It’s also worth noting here that laser-guided 70mm Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System II (APKWS II) rockets, originally designed as air-to-surface munitions, have become the Air Force’s go-to air-to-air weapon against drones. The Air Force, as well as other branches of the U.S. military, have been steadily integrating APKWS II onto a growing number of platforms for use in this role. However, F-35s are not able to employ the rockets at all currently.

Even optimized for the anti-air role, APKWS II also has major limitations, including the need for the target to be designated (or ‘lazed’) throughout the entire engagement. The rockets cannot aggressively maneuver, either, and therefore can only engage steady flying, non-reactionary, low-performance targets. The number of rapid engagements a fighter can execute in a given period is also limited due to the need to acquire and laser each target while getting into very close proximity of it so the rocket can reach. With all this in mind, Air Force F-16 fighters have been spotted in the Middle East in recent years carrying mixed loads of APKWS IIs, AIM-9Xs, and/or AIM-9Ms.

Older and newer Sidewinders are clearly still playing a major role in combat operations in the Middle East, in general. This was underscored just recently by the release of pictures showing a U.S. Marine Corps F/A-18D Hornet in the region loaded with AIM-9Ms and AIM-9Xs, as well as AIM-120 Advanced Medium Range Air-to-Air missiles (AMRAAM). Back in April, at the height of combat operations against Iran, our own Tyler Rogoway highlighted how valuable Marine F/A-18C/Ds with their new AN/APG-79(V)4 active electronically scanned array radars could be, particularly in the counter-drone role.

At this time, we cannot definitively say what the new paint job spotted on AIM-9Xs loaded on Air Force F-35As flying in the Middle East signifies. Still, signs now do point to the further evolution of an already very capable design.

items.titel: BAE Hägglunds lands record $6B deal for 400+ CV90s from five NATO nations
items.anriss: The joint procurement by Finland, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden is expressly linked to the threat from Russia.

absaetze.t: STOCKHOLM — After months of waiting, BAE Systems Hägglunds has finally landed contracts totaling $6 billion (€5.5 billion) to supply more than 400 CV90 infantry fighting vehicles (IFV) in a joint procurement by Finland, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden.

“It’s the biggest deal we [have] ever done, and actually number two in Swedish history of signing international contracts,” Tommy Gustafsson-Rask, general manager at BAE Systems Hägglunds, told Breaking Defense on the sidelines of the signing ceremony in the Swedish capital today.

The joint deal, inked by the five nations for the CV9035 MkIV — dubbed the Nordic Edition — is a clear response to countries concerned about Russia’s threat to NATO’s northern flank. Sweden’s Defense Material Administration (FMV) has signed the main contract with BAE Systems Hägglunds, with each country then signing off on its own deal.

“Deliveries will start in [2029] and then commence in a couple of years after that,” Gustafsson-Rask said, declining to go into exact details about production capacity per year. “But we talk many hundreds [per year],” he added. The chassis hull structures will all be welded at BAE Hägglunds’ Örnsköldsvik facility, but then “chassis assembly, turret welding, turret assembly will be done in the different nations.”

“Then they [nations] have some, as we call them, selectable options. That’s typically their own radio system, their soldier equipment. Then there are some technical options that can be mounted or integrated depending on how they decide,” he added.

The contracts inked today follows last years formalized intention by the five countries and Estonia at a NATO defence ministers’ meeting in Brussels. Estonia withdrew from the plans earlier this year, stating that it needs to prioritizeprefers to prioritise air defense systems and will instead upgrade its existing fleet of roughly 50 CV90s.

The common CV90 Nordic Edition configuration is expected to generate “synergies beneficial to development, spare-parts lead times, integrated logistic support, sustainment and operations,” according to a BAE statement. Shared design features between the Nordic Edition and previous designs are also being touted as a selling point by the company.
Sweden is procuring “about 60” vehicles, valued at 8–10 billion Swedish kronor ($700-$970 million), according to Defense Minister Pål Jonson.

“This is going to be very important for our mechanized brigades to get this capability,” Jonson told Breaking Defense, adding that Sweden donated 50 of its older CV90s to Ukraine in 2024, and previously replenished them with an order to fill up the stocks, in addition to today’s announcement.

Mikael Granholm, the general manager of Sweden’s FMV, seemed to take a more conservative approach regarding when the first deliveries of the 400-plus CV90s could begin. Those would be “starting in 2030 and going on until 2033” he told Breaking Defense while standing next to a CV90 on display outside the Army Museum, where the signing ceremony was completed.

Lithuania is ordering “a little bit more than 100” new CV90s, its defense minister, Robertas Kaunas, said on the sidelines to Breaking Defense, while stressing that speed of delivery is important to counter the Russian threat.

“It’s crucial for us to receive as much as possible until 2030, because we are building our national division, and our national division should be ready till 2030,” he said. The Lithuanian contract is worth around $1.3 billion, he stated.
“It does build military strength, deterrence first of all, and this is [a] reaction to the war that Russia started in Ukraine. We don’t have any different options,” Kaunas said.

Lithuania is the only nation of the five that does not currently operate versions of the tracked CV90. Rather, it operates Boxer wheeled infantry fighting vehicles made by Germany’s ARTEC, a joint venture between KNDS and Rheinmetall.

“This asset [CV9035 MkIV Nordic Edition] enhances our firepower and creates capability to stand firm on the ground and creates capability to all NATO to enhance eastern flank defence and deterrence,” Kaunas said.

Finland confirmed Thursday that it will buy 160 of the more than 400 CV90s for the Finnish Army. The Finnish contract covers the vehicles, spare parts, maintenance kits, testing equipment, technical documentation, training and licenses, together with an option for an additional 100 vehicles. Finland’s project is budgeted at €2.8 billion, with a portion of the funding expected to come from loans under the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) instrument, for deliveries in 2029 and 2030.

Norway is purchasing 70 CV90s, with an option to acquire four more later. The vehicles are scheduled for delivery between 2030 and 2034 and will be used by Brigade Nord and the Finnmark Brigade on the Northern flank, according to the country’s acquisition agency. There were no details further made public by Friday.
The Dutch side of the deal has been kept mostly under wraps, with no details made public immediately at the signing.

BAE Systems’ CV90 infantry fighting vehicle sits in the 20–38-ton class that can integrate a wide range of weapon systems. More than 2,300 vehicles have been ordered by 11 European nations (nine of them NATO members). The vehicles have seen combat experience in Afghanistan and Ukraine, and BAE Systems Hägglunds has invested roughly $450 million to expand production capacity in Örnsköldsvik, per the company.

items.titel: Ahead of Taiwan local elections, politicians crowd in at Art Taipei
items.anriss: 127 galleries took part in the fair at Taipei World Trade Center

absaetze.t: This year's edition of Taiwan's 34-year-old fair Art Taipei (29 October to 2 November) and its third concurrent Taipei Art Week (TAW) fell, serendipitously, just before the alleged spying scandal that emerged around Taiwan's celebrated native son, the naturalised American Nvidia mogul Jensen Huang. This spared fair sales the ensuing worldwide tech stock dive. Rather, concerns during the fair focused more on the pending midterm elections on 28 November.

The fair's opening ceremony was thick with politicians. Prominent figures included incumbent Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an, now in a close re-election race, who would days later face protests at the Taipei Pride parade and festival over his police department's aggressive raid of gay bar Commander D on 3 October. Taiwan's minister of culture Li Yuan heralded his department's successful efforts in September to get a pavilion at the Gwangju Biennale named for Taiwan rather than the sponsoring institution, which sparked a diplomatic row with mainland China, and pronounced that "AI will not replace artists!"

"The presence of political figures at art fairs is a familiar feature of Taiwan's cultural landscape," says Claudia Chen, director of Art Taipei, chair of its organiser, the Taipei Art Gallery Association (Taga), and cofounder of Taipei's Liang Gallery. She adds that it builds public visibility and engagement for the cultural sector. "We hope this attention can help deepen public understanding of the art market and highlight its close connections with cultural development, urban growth, and international exchange."

The question, she continues, "is whether this engagement with political leaders can translate into consistent policy support, particularly in areas such as arts education, international promotion, and incentives for private collecting and cultural patronage." Taiwan lags behind most East Asian governments in cultural investment. "We hope cultural development can become an important public issue and receive sustained support across political parties, allowing Taiwan to gradually translate its economic strength into a deeper and more far-reaching cultural influence."

Chen says that Taiwan's technology sector and the private wealth it fuels "provide an important foundation for its art market. However, translating economic growth into greater activity in the art market takes time," as well as innovation and outreach by galleries.

The 127 galleries that Art Taipei welcomed to the Taipei World Trade Center this year included the return of influential galleries such as Richard Koh Fine Art, from Kuala Lumpur and Singapore, for the first time post-pandemic, and Perrotin for a third consecutive year. Newcomers included Tokyo's Misako & Rosen. One of Taipei's leading platforms, Tina Keng Gallery (TKG+) and TKG+ Projects, joined for the first time in about five years. "In recent years, with Singapore, Seoul, Hong Kong, there is a lot happening, so we needed an opportunity to do a Taiwan show," says the gallery's assistant to the director, Alice Liang. With the suspension of the sleeker international fair Taipei Dangdai after 2025, Art Taipei has resumed its status as the main "hometown" option, she says.

Sales of a "museum-type" installation of works by artists including Sanyu, Kuo Tzumin and Michael Lin went "pretty well", says Liang. "People were surprised and curious," with "positive feedback" from collectors who skewed young and were both Taiwanese and foreign. She adds that the launch of the broader art week had little impact on sales, "but we can feel the difference, with the events, parties and open studios."

Fair organisers also report a generational shift among buyers, with 20.8% of those surveyed saying they were attending for the first or second time, double the figure for 2023. VIP collectors also declined from 77.5% to 54.2%, suggesting that the publicly accessible side of the art week is also providing outreach for the fair. Endeavours included five bus rounds, guided tours, digital art screenings at Taipei Lumitree and 30 public artworks displayed citywide, says Chen. For the art industry, a forum included speakers such as M+ Hong Kong curator Russell Storer and 2026 Venice Biennale Korea Pavilion curator Binna Choi.

The fair also featured an expanded presence of galleries from Korea and Japan, with 25 and 22 respectively, drawing on Taga's ongoing collaboration with those countries' gallery associations. Galleries from Japan, Taiwan's former coloniser, "have maintained a longstanding presence in the Taiwanese market, with many having established strong collector networks and brand recognition over the years," says Chen. The Korean presence "demonstrates the Korean art industry's capacity to expand into international markets through collaboration."

Tastes at the fair are also shifting towards Pop and contemporary art, says dealer Steven Chen (no relation). His Taipei gallery Yiyun Art has attended the fair for seven of the past ten years. It represents traditional Asian paintings, which remain a major sector at Art Taipei, if reduced from previous years. His dramatic maze of a booth, evoking a Chinese scholar's garden, saw steady crowds and sales, including of a painting by Yu Cheng Yao for $90,000. "With the young generation is coming more to the fair," says Chen, "we need a new language on ink art. It is the same culture with a new expression."

Claudia Chen says that Taiwan's collectors are maintaining "purchasing momentum" but have become increasingly deliberate, needing time and established relationships with galleries. Meanwhile, younger collectors are "gradually entering the market, bringing more diverse perspectives shaped by their own lifestyles and aesthetic preferences."

items.titel: Programa extension brings SketchUp models and product schedules into one workflow
items.anriss: Studio operations software Programa has introduced a SketchUp extension that connects 3D models with its product Schedules, freeing designers from duplicating information and giving them more creative time.

absaetze.t: Studio operations software Programa has introduced a SketchUp extension that connects 3D models with its product Schedules, freeing designers from duplicating information and giving them more creative time.
According to Programa, the extension is designed to reduce duplicate data entry by connecting a 3D model in SketchUp with a project’s Schedule in Programa.
Programa’s Schedules function acts as a streamlined alternative to spreadsheets, detailing each item’s code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.
The extension runs inside SketchUp and allows designers to link components in the model to matching products in the Schedule.
As a result, designers can track an item from the first 3D sketch through to its final specification, without entering the same information separately in SketchUp and Programa.
From the model, designers can send a component to a chosen Schedule, or link it to a product that is already listed there.
Programa explained that linking to an existing product creates a connection without adding a duplicate line item, keeping the Schedule “clean” as the design is fleshed out.
Before anything is added, designers can review and edit the product’s information.
The Schedule entry combines the details available from the component with anything entered during that review.
Programa said this gives studios a chance to check the specification before it is used for pricing or procurement.
The extension also provides access to Programa’s Product Library within SketchUp.
Designers can place saved 3D models directly into their designs, and use product images as material swatches to bring selected finishes into the model.
In this way, the products (and finishes) a studio has chosen can be seen in the visuals as well as listed in the Schedule.
The process also works in reverse, starting from the Schedule. A product with a compatible 3D model attached can be placed straight into SketchUp.
If there is no model, designers can choose a stand-in from SketchUp’s 3D Warehouse, or from elsewhere in the current model, to represent the product.
Once a component and a product are connected, supported changes can be reviewed and applied in either direction.
For example, adding another copy of a connected chair in SketchUp generates a quantity change, which the designer can then apply to the Schedule.
The company added that changes are presented for review “before the corresponding update is applied”.
This means the model and the specification can move together as a design develops, while the Schedule is only updated once the designer has chosen to apply a change.
Programa stressed that responsibility remains with the studio.
Designers stay in charge of “selecting the right product, checking its details and deciding when the model or Schedule should change”, the company said.
The aim, it explained, is to carry information between the model and the specification rather than make those decisions on the designer’s behalf.
The extension is aimed at studios that model in SketchUp and manage their specifications in Programa.
The Programa extension works with SketchUp desktop on Mac and Windows.
To learn more, visit Programa’s website or its extension setup guide.

items.titel: Notes from the underground: Why you should dig deep to find your people
items.anriss: The underground carpark is alive with the sound of music ( writes Blake Matich ). Yodelling, to be specific. Herders and farmers have long used the Alpine practice to talk shop across valleys of old and pastures new. But in Graz, Austria, …

absaetze.t: Culture
November 27, 2026
3 Min Read
There’s more than vocal flips and falsettos to be found in the depths of a subterranean yodelling class. Far below the mainstream, you might just find something more profound: your tribe.

The underground carpark is alive with the sound of music (writes Blake Matich). Yodelling, to be specific. Herders and farmers have long used the Alpine practice to talk shop across valleys of old and pastures new. But in Graz, Austria, where the relatively flat surroundings of the Grazerfeld plain are not as echo-friendly as hills and mountains, a group of some 30 yodellers have found an acoustic alternative – and friendship, presumably – in the subterranean Kastner & Öhler parking garage.

Yodelling isn’t the first thing that comes to mind when you think of underground scenes, literal or metaphorical. In my twenties, going “underground” meant partying in a former public toilet beneath a Berlin intersection or dodging stalactites rum-drunk as I descended into La Cueva, a cavernous club within a Cuban hillside. No sooner had I sunk to the nadir of this discoteca in a natural cave and double-parked myself with a fresh pair of cuba libres than I noticed a woman sat on a table, draped in snakes, surrounded by four scantily-clad dancers who proceeded to lift said table using only their mouths (a corner each). You know, the kind of good, clean, cave-dwelling hijinks that you hope to find in the nether regions.

But now that I’m making good progress in my thirties, it’s nice to know that there are scenes that aren’t a bog-standard toilet rave or a snake cave. These days, I make more modest descents and following the sound of the underground usually finds me improvising comedic riffs in the basement of a King’s Cross church or sipping mocktails in the sort of Bertie Wooster-style speakeasies that always seem a police whistle away from being raided by truncheon-wielding bobbies. Anyone fancy a piña no-lada at The Jaundiced Newt?
Still, it’s nice to know that, despite an increasingly homogenised world, exploring underground and alternative scenes is still a bona fide way to find your people – even if they’re yodellers.

Some scenes don’t even necessitate a dip below the surface. In Japan, the lure of the underground meets cultural restraint in the form of “manholers”. Get your head out of the gutter – we’re talking about a community of enthusiasts for the creatively illustrated manhole covers that put a colourful lid on the country’s sewer system. If you’re looking for a weird niche, Japan has you covered.

Even just finding a good book club can be an ordeal. Some are so underground that they don’t even exist. A Vanity Fair investigation by Clara Molot published this week exposed the International Institute of Literature & Arts (IILA), a prestigious society of literature scholars. The esteemed professors listed among its fellows should have known better than to judge a book by its cover. The IILA is, in all likelihood, a Chinese intelligence op. When asked to comment on the IILA, a Chinese embassy spokesman said: “I am not familiar with the specific situation that you mentioned.” Translated from diplomacy talk, this means: The first rule of the International Institute of Literature & Arts is that you do not talk about the International Institute of Literature & Arts.

International conspiracies aside, the modern world seems intent on housing us in silos. Thankfully we’re free to dig tunnels between them. Can’t find the club, class or community that fits the bill? Never fear – there’s no shortage of niches and crannies underground. Whether you’re yearning to yodel or want to join the ranks of the academic literati for the small price of a membership fee and eternal fealty to the Chinese Communist Party, there’s an underground scene for you. Your people are out there. You might just have to dig deep to find them.

items.titel: Exposition à Aix-en-Provence : en 2027, l’hôtel de Caumont racontera la folle histoire de la couleur en peinture, de Monet à Matisse

absaetze.t: Monet, Caillebotte, Seurat… L’année prochaine, Caumont – Centre d’art à Aix-en-Provence présentera une exposition inédite sur la révolution de la couleur qui s’est opérée de la fin du XIXe au début du XXe siècles.

2027 promet déjà d’être riche en expositions fascinantes ! Du 23 avril au 3 octobre, Caumont – Centre d’art à Aix-en-Provence organisera « De Monet à Matisse, une révolution en couleurs ». Avec une soixantaine d’œuvres de Boudin, Monet, Renoir ou encore Matisse, l’événement retracera près d’un siècle d’évolution de la couleur en peinture, de la seconde moitié du XIXe au début du XXe siècle. La commissaire de l’exposition Marianne Mathieu racontera cette histoire en trois parties chronologiques, des impressionnistes aux fauves, en passant par les néo-impressionnistes.
Le plein air des impressionnistes et leurs maîtres

L’exposition s’ouvrira sur une première section consacrée aux impressionnistes et leurs maîtres. Dès le milieu du XIXe siècle, certains artistes quittent l’atelier pour peindre en plein air grâce à des innovations techniques. Dans les années 1860, les peintures sont produites en masse et conditionnées en tubes. Qui plus est, la multiplication des teintes issues de la chimie permet aux artistes de travailler différemment. Eugène Boudin, Camille Corot et Johan Barthold Jongkind mais aussi les impressionnistes Claude Monet, Auguste Renoir ou encore Gustave Caillebotte, vont ainsi rechercher en extérieur une peinture de la lumière. À l’occasion de l’exposition, les visiteurs pourront contempler des œuvres inédites comme Aux petites dalles (1884) de Monet, jamais montrée en France, et Saules de Caillebotte, révélée pour la première fois au public.
Claude Monet, Les Sapins à Varengeville, 1882, huile sur toile, 60 x 73 cm. Photo © Christie’s Images / Bridgeman Images
Les expérimentations de Seurat, Signac et les néo-impressionnistes

La deuxième section de l’exposition se concentrera sur le tournant néo-impressionniste et l’étude de la couleur. À la suite des travaux du chimiste Michel-Eugène Chevreul, dont la loi du contraste simultané, qui décrit la manière dont les couleurs s’influencent et se modifient lorsqu’elles sont juxtaposées, les néo-impressionnistes expérimentent les sciences de la couleur. Les œuvres de Seurat ou Signac par exemple jouent avec notre perception optique. Les deux artistes utilisent ainsi des touches de couleurs pures pour créer une nouvelle couleur, visible uniquement de loin.
Paul Signac, Voiles et pins, 1896, huile sur toile, 81 x 52 cm, collection particulière. Photo © Heritage Images / Fine Art Images / akg-images
La couleur pure libérée de Matisse et des fauves

La troisième section abordera les audacieuses peintures des fauves où la couleur devient un sujet à part entière. Après les néo-impressionnistes, une nouvelle génération d’artistes découvre une autre voie : celle de la libération de la couleur vive. Des artistes comme Henri Matisse vont rendre visite à Signac et Henri-Edmond Cross à Saint-Tropez et vont s’inspirer de leurs explorations picturales pour aller plus loin. Matisse, Maurice de Vlaminck, André Derain, Albert Marquet ou encore Raoul Dufy vont s’éloigner du réel pour utiliser les couleurs directement sortie du tube, en aplats expressifs et exaltants.
Henri Matisse, Côte de Belle-Île-en-Mer, 1896, huile sur toile, 85,5 x 65,7 cm, collection particulière, France. Photo © Jean-Louis Losi, Paris

Bords de Seine à Bougival (1906) Maurice de Vlaminck, Paysage de l’Estaque de Georges Braque (1906) et La Bottine jaune (1909) de Kees van Dongen seront présentées dans l’exposition pour montrer que chez les fauves, les couleurs pures priment sur la lumière. « Matisse est l’artiste qui incarne par excellence cette recherche, explique le centre d’art dans un communiqué. Ses figures des années vingt et trente en sont l’une des expressions les plus séduisantes, tandis que les papiers découpés en sont l’expression ultime et paradigmatique. » Enfin, un épilogue sur le blanc et les pigments or clôturera l’exposition autour d’une œuvre de l’artiste franco-américaine Vicky Colombet, produite à cette occasion.
En 2025, le Grimaldi Forum consacrait également une exposition aux couleurs dans l’histoire de l’art :

En 2025, une autre exposition avait également choisi la couleur comme sujet principale. En collaboration avec le Musée national d’Art moderne, le Grimaldi Forum avait présenté les chefs-d’œuvre du Centre Pompidou pour retracer l’histoire de l’art du XXe siècle en 7 couleurs. Le temps d’un été, l’exposition proposait des dialogues inattendus et une relecture inédite des collections nationales dans un cercle chromatique géant. Il ne reste plus qu’à attendre quelques mois pour découvrir si Caumont – Centre d’art osera une scénographie aussi audacieuse.
